description: I’m a software developer with a growing interest in farming. I’m starting a team for Field Shift to build a practical tool that helps farmers compare crop rotations using NASA data, local soil information, and their own priorities. I’m currently a team of one and would love to work with people who are passionate builders, creatives as well as designers and storytellers. You don’t need to know everything—let’s build and learn together.
summary:
Limeni is a free web app that helps Zambian farmers choose a crop rotation that fits their land, their rainfall and their market. Most smallholders grow maize season after season. That drains the soil and leaves families exposed when the rains fail, as they did in the 2023/24 El Niño drought.

A farmer taps their field on a map. Limeni then pulls 45 years of NASA and NASA-partner Earth data for that spot:

CHIRPS daily rainfall via NASA SERVIR
NASA POWER heat and root-zone soil moisture
NASA SRTM slope
NASA GIBS satellite map layers

It turns this into a picture of the local season: when rains reliably start, how often droughts and dry spells happen, and how risky the heat is. Limeni scores each rotation of 11 local crops on weather fit, drought safety, soil health, pest break, erosion and market value. It shows the farmer’s current practice, a common local rotation and the best match, each with a farming calendar and plain-language reasons. Farmers can add their own crop prices and upload a soil test photo or PDF to refine the results.

Limeni turns NASA data into decisions a first-time farmer can understand and act on, on any phone.
details:
What it does
Limeni (from a local word for farming) helps smallholder farmers in Zambia plan a three-season crop rotation that matches their local climate, soil and market. It is built for first-time farmers on a phone. It first explains what crop rotation is and why it matters, and “I’m just starting out” is an accepted answer.

How it works

  1. Find your farm. Tap anywhere in Zambia on the map, or search for a place. Limeni fetches daily rainfall from 1981 to today for that spot from CHIRPS (via NASA SERVIR ClimateSERV), and temperature and root-zone soil moisture from NASA POWER. It also samples NASA SRTM elevation around the point to estimate slope.
    • when the rains reliably start (20 mm over 3 days with no 10-day dry spell after)
    • when they end
    • total rainfall
    • mid-season dry spells
    • hot days above 32 °C
    • drought years (under 75% of the median)
    • weather fit
    • rain safety
    • soil health (legumes, organic matter, ground cover on slopes)
    • pest and disease break
    • ease of selling
  2. Make it yours. Farmers can enter today’s and expected harvest prices from their buyer, and upload a photo or PDF of a soil test. Limeni reads pH, texture and organic carbon from it, and the farmer confirms the values. A “what if the rains get weaker or stronger” slider shows how options hold up under climate change. An AI-written summary explains the result using only the numbers on the page, with a fixed-text fallback.

Why we chose CHIRPS for rainfall
We first used NASA POWER’s model rainfall, but it showed the 2023/24 season in southern Zambia as normal when it was a severe drought. So we tested three rainfall sources against the 2018/19 and 2023/24 droughts. CHIRPS, which blends satellite estimates with rain gauges, was the only one that caught both, so we chose it.

Results

  • Growing maize every season scores lowest in all three test areas (dry south, central, wet north).
  • In dry Sinazongwe, the best rotation drops maize for pearl millet, soybean and cowpea.
  • Further north, it keeps maize and adds legumes.
  • With 20% less rain, drought years in Sinazongwe nearly double (9 to 17 of 45) and maize-only scores fall, while drought-hardy rotations still hold up.

Benefits and intended impact
Limeni helps farmers:

  • diversify away from maize monoculture
  • lower their drought risk
  • rebuild soil with legumes
  • protect sloping land from erosion
  • weigh market value with their own prices

It gives extension officers a free, explainable tool to use in conversations with farmers. It is a support tool, not a replacement for local advice, and every result says so.

Tools and technologies

  • App: Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel.
  • Maps and charts: Leaflet maps, Recharts charts, Photon (OpenStreetMap) place search.
  • AI: DeepSeek API for the plain-language summary and for reading soil reports.
  • NASA and partner data: CHIRPS via NASA SERVIR ClimateSERV, NASA POWER API, NASA SRTM (via OpenTopoData), NASA GIBS WMTS map tiles.
  • Other data: FAO ECOCROP, plus Zambian crop prices and yields from public market and ministry sources.
  • Code: open source at https://github.com/Elyumusa/Limeni.
